title: How Vomit Phobia Works
summary: Hosts Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explain metaphobia, the specific phobia of vomiting, listed in the DSM. They cover how it differs from ordinary disgust and from fear of vomiting, its rough prevalence (under one percent, about four women to one man), and how it often starts with a traumatic childhood vomiting experience and resembles PTSD. Josh shares a childhood bus story about a classmate who made himself vomit. They describe how the phobia spirals into avoidance, hypervigilance, checking behavior, restricted diets, agoraphobia, and carrying emergency bags, and how anxiety itself can cause queasiness. A case study of an eight-year-old girl with appendicitis is discussed. Treatments covered include CBT, exposure and response prevention, gradual exposure (including the rate my vomit website), and EMDR. The episode closes with a listener mail story about a dog that suffocated in a chip bag.
topics: EMDR eye movement desensitization and reprocessing

entities.name: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders

segments.title: Introduction to metaphobia
segments.summary: Hosts warn listeners the episode is gross and introduce metaphobia as a specific phobia of vomiting listed in the DSM. They distinguish it from general disgust and from the milder fear of vomiting, and mention a listener's story about overcoming it.

segments.title: Prevalence and onset of metaphobia
segments.summary: The hosts say study is limited, estimate that under one percent of people have metaphobia with about four women for each man, and describe it as a chronic condition that often begins after a traumatic vomiting experience in childhood and resembles PTSD. Josh shares a childhood bus story about a classmate who made himself vomit.

segments.title: How the phobia develops and affects life
segments.summary: The hosts describe how fear spreads from seeing vomit to fearing one's own vomiting, leading to hypervigilance, avoidance, and a panic attack when the word is encountered. They note that people with the phobia are statistically less likely to vomit than others, and that the anticipation drives the fear.

segments.title: Irony of anxiety and nausea
segments.summary: The hosts explain the irony that worrying about vomiting causes anxiety, which can make a person feel queasy, though anxiety cannot actually cause vomiting. They advise telling oneself that queasiness is not nausea that leads to vomiting.

segments.title: Behavioral effects and restrictions
segments.summary: The hosts list behaviors that people with metaphobia adopt: avoiding handshakes, TV vomit scenes, and certain foods; checking food; eating only safe foods; carrying emergency bags and change of clothes; avoiding travel and alcohol; and developing agoraphobia, sometimes confused with it. They also mention avoiding pregnancy out of fear of morning sickness.

segments.title: Eight-year-old appendicitis case study
segments.summary: The hosts describe a case study of an eight-year-old girl who vomited from appendicitis before surgery and then developed metaphobia, fearing vomiting, avoiding outside food and other children, and fearing her father's travel.

segments.title: Treatment: CBT, exposure therapy, and EMDR
segments.summary: The hosts cover treatments including CBT and exposure and response prevention. Methods include saying the word vomit, looking at fake vomit, making gagging sounds, home exposure with homemade vomit, and the rate my vomit website. They then describe EMDR, which uses guided eye movements while recalling a trauma.

segments.title: Listener mail: dog suffocation
segments.summary: A listener named Jackie W from Seattle writes about losing their dog River, who suffocated after getting its head stuck in a chip bag left on the counter. The hosts urge listeners to keep bags put away and cut the bottoms off bags before recycling.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listeners to send personal stories of phobias and share contact details for the show.
